title: Mastery Challenge: Computers & the Internet
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Computers & the Internet Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: bits, drive sizes, pixels, gates, the processor, memory, speeds, AI, quantum, chips and checking claims. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Computers & the Internet Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from a single bit to judging a claim about AI. Level 1 followed one photo through the machine; now see how far you've come. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Computers & the Internet: mastered
learned: How a computer stores text, pictures and sound as bits and works on them with gates and a processor.
How to turn an advertised speed or drive size into what you'll actually get.
Why claims about AI, quantum computers and chips need a task, a date and a source.
Which three questions sort most tech claims: how it works, who says so, what it costs.

questions.prompt: A new 2 TB drive shows up in Windows as about 1,862 GB. What explains it?

options.label: The drive is faulty and has lost some of its bytes
options.rationale: No bytes are missing.

options.label: Windows uses bigger, 1,024-based gigabytes to count the same bytes
The maker rounded its label up by about 138 GB
options.rationale: It really holds two trillion bytes.

options.label: A hidden system backup took up the missing space
options.rationale: The gap is counting, not files.

questions.explanation: The drive holds two trillion bytes; Windows' 1,024-based gigabytes show that as about 1,862 GB, twice 931.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does it take to store the colors of 10 pixels?

options.rationale: Each pixel needs three bytes, one per color.
That counts bits for 10 bytes.
That is the patterns in one byte.

questions.explanation: Each pixel needs one byte each for red, green and blue: 3 × 10 = 30 bytes.

questions.prompt: A porch light should turn on if motion is sensed or the manual switch is on. Which gate does that job?

options.label: OR
AND
options.rationale: AND would need both at once.

options.label: NOT
options.rationale: NOT flips one input.

options.label: No gate can
options.rationale: A single OR gate does it.

questions.explanation: OR outputs 1 when any input is 1.

questions.prompt: What does a processor do as soon as it finishes executing an instruction?

options.label: Switches itself off to cool down
options.rationale: The cycle simply starts over.

options.label: Starts the cycle again with the next instruction
Deletes that instruction from memory for good
options.rationale: Instructions stay in memory.

options.label: Waits for the user to press a key before going on
options.rationale: It keeps looping on its own.

questions.explanation: When one instruction is executed, fetch, decode and execute begin again with the next.

questions.prompt: Why don't computers build all their memory from fast SRAM?

options.label: SRAM forgets everything it holds once every second
options.rationale: The problem is size and cost.

options.label: SRAM can only store text, not numbers or pictures
options.rationale: It stores any bits.

options.label: SRAM takes much more space, so the same chip holds several times as much DRAM
SRAM is slower than the storage that keeps your files
options.rationale: SRAM is the fastest layer after registers.

questions.explanation: SRAM is fast but physically large, so memory comes in layers from small, fast cache to roomy, slower DRAM and storage.

questions.prompt: Your plan is 400 Mbps. At best, how many megabytes per second can you download?

options.rationale: That treats bits as bytes.
That multiplies by 8 instead of dividing.
That divides by 4, not 8.

questions.explanation: Divide megabits by 8: 400 ÷ 8 = 50 megabytes per second.

questions.prompt: A headline says an AI aced a math contest, so it can surely handle your spreadsheet. What's the best response?

options.label: Agree: math skill means it's good at everything
options.rationale: AI's abilities are jagged.

options.label: Judge it on your own task, and check when its abilities were measured
Disagree: AI can't do math at all
options.rationale: It reached olympiad gold in 2025.

options.label: Only trust AI on tasks it has never been tested on
options.rationale: Tested tasks are where you have evidence.

questions.explanation: AI's frontier is jagged: success on one task says little about the next, and abilities change fast.

questions.prompt: Which headline about quantum computers and encryption is the most accurate?

options.label: Quantum computers have already broken all of today's encryption
options.rationale: No such machine is known to exist yet.

options.label: Quantum threatens public-key methods like RSA; post-quantum standards are out
Quantum computers will make every kind of encryption unbreakable
options.rationale: They threaten some of today's methods.

options.label: Today's encryption will stay safe forever, whatever happens
options.rationale: Public-key methods would fall to a large quantum computer.

questions.explanation: A large quantum computer would break RSA and elliptic-curve methods; NIST released post-quantum standards in 2024.

questions.prompt: Clock rates stopped climbing in the mid-2000s. What did chipmakers add to get more work done for the same power?

options.label: A much faster clock
options.rationale: Faster clocks cost too much power and heat.

options.label: More cores that share the work
Slower, cheaper memory
options.rationale: Slower memory makes processors wait.

options.label: Larger, brighter screens
options.rationale: Screens don't speed up processing.

questions.explanation: Splitting work across cores at a lower clock rate gives more performance for the same power.

questions.prompt: A viral post says phones secretly record everything for ads. Asking 'who says so?', what's the strongest evidence to weigh?

options.label: The number of likes and shares the post has collected
options.rationale: Popularity isn't evidence.

options.label: An ad from a company selling a privacy app
options.rationale: Sellers have something to sell.

options.label: A 2018 university test of 17,000+ apps that found no secret audio sending
A friend's spooky story about an ad after a chat
options.rationale: One story can't test the claim.

questions.explanation: Independent researchers tested thousands of apps and found none secretly sending audio, though they couldn't test every phone.
